extracted.intended_audience: law students and patent practitioners (U.S. patent eligibility §101)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and applying U.S. §101 subject-matter eligibility rules and related case law (e.g., Chakrabarty, Mayo, Myriad, Diehr, Alice) to inventions in biotechnology, diagnostics, software, and business methods. Focus is on determining whether claims are directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas and whether they include sufficient additional features to be patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §101 statutory scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory text is the starting point for eligibility analysis; Congress used broad language and intended §101 to have wide scope (e.g., 'anything under the sun that is made by man'). The statute is nevertheless interpreted in light of judicially recognized exceptions and subsequent case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat these categories as implicit exceptions because they are the basic tools of scientific and technological work; granting patents that monopolize them risks inhibiting future innovation. However, the exceptions must be applied carefully so as not to eviscerate patent law, since all inventions at some level embody natural laws or abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of human-made, non-naturally occurring manufactures/compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-made organisms or compositions that are not products of nature qualify as patentable subject matter (e.g., Chakrabarty: a genetically engineered bacterium held patentable as a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consult ordinary definitions of 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter' (production of articles for use; compositions of two or more substances) and emphasize human ingenuity: if the claimed subject matter has distinctive name, character, and use and is not merely nature's handiwork, it can be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring things are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Products that exist in nature (e.g., a new mineral found in the earth, a plant found in the wild, unmodified naturally occurring DNA) are treated as products of nature and not patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation alone does not necessarily make a natural product patentable; courts look to whether the item is 'markedly different' from what exists in nature (Myriad) and whether claiming it would improperly appropriate nature's handiwork into private ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility of cDNA (synthetic DNA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary DNA (cDNA), which is synthetically created and not naturally occurring, is patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: cDNA differs from natural DNA because introns are removed; because it is not a product that exists in nature, it can be eligible subject matter. Distinguish between unmodified genomic DNA (ineligible) and synthetic constructs (eligible) based on natural occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework (directed-to and inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; Step 2: if so, consider whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim simply recites the law and adds conventional activity, it fails step 2. Courts apply precedent (Mayo, Diehr, Flook) to decide whether the additional elements integrate the law into a patent-eligible application or merely attempt to monopolize the law itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept must be significantly more than routine or conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional claim features must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers in the field in order to supply the 'inventive concept' required under Mayo step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo held that routine testing/observations or standard data-gathering steps cannot convert a claim directed to a natural law into patent-eligible subject matter. By contrast, nonconventional combinations or technological improvements may suffice (see Diehr, DDR, Bascom, Amdocs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption as a key evaluative concern
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that would effectively monopolize a natural law, abstract idea, or basic tool of science (thereby foreclosing others from using it) is suspect and likely unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly emphasize the danger of preemption as a rationale for excluding certain claims; analyses often ask whether the patent would 'tie up' the use of underlying principles and inhibit future innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation / machine-or-transformation indicia of eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of a law/formula within a transformative process or via a specific machine (e.g., Diehr's rubber-molding process using the Arrhenius equation implemented by a computer controlling the press) supports patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a sole test, showing that a mathematical formula or natural law is integrated into a practical application (installation, continuous monitoring, automatic control) can demonstrate that the claim is 'significantly more' than the law itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to vs application distinction and the draftsman's-art warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts caution against allowing patent eligibility to 'depend simply on the draftsman's art'—i.e., dressing an ineligible law in application language to claim it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flook, Alice, and related authorities warn that merely appending 'apply it' or adding conventional steps will not render a claim eligible. Examiners and courts will look beyond form to substance to determine whether the claim truly claims an application or merely the law itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA §33 prohibition on patents directed to human organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The America Invents Act §33 states: 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory limitation removes human organisms from patent eligibility; the PTO has advised applicants to include 'non-human' limitations where appropriate. The precise scope of 'human organism' can be a contested interpretive question.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO drafting guidance for claims touching human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO guidance: 'A claim directed to or including within its scope a human being will not be considered to be patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101' and suggests adding a 'non-human' limitation where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is administrative guidance for claim drafting to avoid a ground of rejection; negative limitations are a permissible drafting device. Administrative guidance does not change statutory text but affects examiner practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and business-method eligibility—'rooted in computer technology' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions, claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to solve a problem specifically arising in computer networks or that provide an unconventional technological solution may be eligible (e.g., DDR Holdings, Bascom, Amdocs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between merely performing a conventional business practice on the Internet (likely abstract) and inventing a technical solution to Internet-centric problems (more likely to carry an inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer or Internet implementation insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting generic computer components or performing a business method 'on the Internet' does not by itself transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter (Ultramercial, Alice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will scrutinize whether the computer implementation contributes any unconventional technological feature beyond routine use of the Internet or computers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated examples of ineligible subject matter formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and the PTO use alternative phrasings for the exceptions: 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'systems that depend on human intelligence alone,' 'disembodied concepts,' 'mental processes,' and 'disembodied mathematical algorithms and formulas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formulations are functionally similar to 'laws of nature,' 'natural phenomena,' and 'abstract ideas.' Practitioners should be mindful that examiners/courts may use varied labels when applying §101 jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of steps into a process can supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that integrates a formula or natural law into additional steps forming a new, practical process—where those steps are not merely conventional—can be patent eligible (Diehr example: continuous temperature monitoring + automatic press control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look to whether the combination as a whole achieves a technological improvement or solves a practical problem in a nonconventional way, rather than merely appending steps to the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality fact-finding in eligibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' in the relevant field is a factual inquiry that affects §101 outcomes (Mayo emphasized that routine lab steps cannot supply the inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence about common practice in the field, prior art, and technical conventionality can be determinative; examiners and courts will consider what was routine at the time of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of policy concerns vs statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts generally decline to resolve broad ethical, social, or environmental policy issues through §101 interpretations and suggest those matters belong to the legislative and executive branches (Chakrabarty discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While policy considerations inform debates about scope, eligibility analysis focuses on statutory construction and precedent; Congress may amend §101 if it wishes to change substantive eligibility boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative (PTO) guidelines vs judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO issues examination guidelines (e.g., 2019 Guidelines) to instruct examiners on applying §101, but such guidelines are not binding law and may diverge from or be less strict than court interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware of PTO practice but recognize that courts, especially the Federal Circuit and Supreme Court, ultimately control legal interpretation; PTO guideline changes can affect examination outcomes and consistency, however.
